publications.title: Real-Time Solution of Quadratic Optimization Problems with Banded Matrices and Indicator Variables
publications.abstract: We consider mixed-integer quadratic optimization problems with banded matrices and indicator variables. These problems arise pervasively in statistical inference problems with time-series data, where the banded matrix captures the temporal relationship of the underlying process. In particular, the problem studied arises in monitoring problems, where the decision-maker wants to detect changes or anomalies. We propose to solve these problems using decision diagrams. In particular we show how to exploit the temporal dependencies to construct exact and approximate decision diagrams. For problems over matrices with bandwidth equal to one, the proposed method runs in polynomial time. Moreover, if the bandwidth and condition number of the matrix is fixed, then we show that the proposed method can be modified to run into an additive approximation scheme. We also describe how to construct the convex hull of the set under study from the decision diagrams, and how to deploy the method online to solve the problems via a shortest path algorithm. Computational experiments show that, for problems with bandwidths less or equal than three, our proposed algorithm compares favorably to a state-of-the-art off-the-shelf solver in the offline setting, and that we are able to solve problems in milliseconds for the online setting.

publications.title: EXPRESS: What Drives Physician Efficiency? Evidence from Emergency Department Operations
publications.abstract:
Emergency department (ED) physicians play a critical role in healthcare, serving on the frontline of acute care delivery. Yet increasing demand, resource constraints, and growing patient complexity pose significant challenges to physician efficiency. In this study, we investigate the determinants of ED physician efficiency using a multi-stage framework. First, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to measure individual physician efficiency based on data from 110,325 patient visits at a leading U.S. hospital. Second, we use a Tobit regression model to analyze how physician experience, shift familiarity, and patient severity influence physician efficiency. Third, we conduct comprehensive robustness checks, including omitted variable bias sensitivity analyses, permutation tests, and machine learning-based classification analyses, to address concerns regarding endogeneity and potential model misspecification.
                  Our results show that physician efficiency increases with experience at a diminishing rate. Efficiency also varies with shift familiarity, with the estimated association weakening as physician experience increases. In addition, higher patient severity is associated with lower physician efficiency, consistent with the greater resource demands of caring for more clinically complex patients. This negative association is attenuated for more experienced physicians, suggesting that experienced physicians are better able to maintain efficiency when managing more demanding clinical conditions. Our findings offer actionable recommendations for improving ED operations. Staffing strategies that assign relatively more experienced physicians to higher-severity patients may help maintain physician efficiency, while shift familiarity may inform a scheduling strategy that emphasizes greater scheduling consistency for relatively less experienced physicians and greater flexibility for relatively more experienced physicians. Simulation results further illustrate the potential reductions in physician resource use associated with these strategies. Together, these findings highlight the value of evidence-based physician staffing and scheduling to improve physician efficiency in EDs.

publications.title: EXPRESS: Harnessing Renewable Portfolio Standards for Sustainable Futures: An Empirical Examination of Spillover Effects
publications.abstract: Given the importance of managing industrial energy consumption, setting standards and implementing policies that encourage renewable energy use is crucial for incentivizing sustainable firm practices. Public policy designs must align closely with firms’ environmental policies to help mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support a sustainable future. While research on policy impacts on firm environmental performance and the supply chain's role in sustainability is growing, a critical, understudied effect is the spillover of government rules to supply chain partners and peer firms, especially those outside the direct purview of environmental regulations. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates data from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS). The latter refers to state-driven initiatives that incentivize electricity consumption from eligible renewable resources. We examine the causal effects of state-level policies on firm-level GHG emission intensity, with particular emphasis on the spillover effects of policies on unregulated firms across markets. We break down emission intensity into Scope 1 and Scope 2 and capture facility-level data to analyze spillover effects in granular detail. Using a staggered difference-in-differences methodology, our analysis finds a promising negative association between RPS introduction and GHG emission intensity among unregulated firms across industries. Interestingly, firms headquartered in states with more conservative initial targets during RPS adoption and progressive, milestone-based implementation strategies have significantly lower GHG emission intensity than those headquartered in states with more aggressive initial targets or long-term absolute targets. Our findings have significant implications for developing environmental regulations and public policies aimed at reducing GHG emission intensity.

publications.title: EXPRESS: Participation Governance in Consumer and AI Co-creation: Whether to Intervene and How to Design It
publications.abstract: Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

publications.title: ARCHITECTURE OF A HOSPITAL INFORMATION SYSTEM BASED ON ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORDS
publications.abstract: Information technologies have become an integral part of healthcare, and the hospital information system (HIS) is their core. Paper records are slow, hard to share and prone to loss and errors. This article proposes a layered architecture of a hospital information system built around a single electronic health record (EHR). The architecture has four levels: user access, functional modules, integration services and a central database. The main modules are patient registration, the electronic health record, laboratory, radiology with image archiving, pharmacy, and management and statistics. Data exchange between modules and with external systems is based on the HL7 FHIR and DICOM standards. Information security is ensured by role-based access, encryption and an audit log. The proposed architecture can serve as a basis for introducing information systems in medical institutions and for teaching medical informatics to students.

publications.title: SILT Core v0.1: Delegation and Revocation Semantics for Federated Research Infrastructure — AUT CISRC Research Pilot
publications.abstract: This research release documents a constrained proof of concept applying SILT Core v0.1 delegation and revocation semantics to federated research infrastructure. Using a synthetic university research-governance workflow associated with the Auckland University of Technology Computer and Information Sciences Research Centre (AUT CISRC), the implementation represents an asserted institutional authority chain, a time-bound delegation, a scoped research-data request and applicable revocation events as machine-readable JSON artefacts. A lightweight Python reference validator evaluates delegation conditions including issuer-chain relationships, actor, permitted action, resource, purpose, temporal validity, expiry and revocation. The Phase 3 automated regression suite passed 21 of 21 tests, including positive and negative scenarios, malformed-input handling and representative JSON Schema validation. The release includes the original SILT Core v0.1 delegation and revocation specifications, a non-normative AUT CISRC implementation profile, five profile-specific JSON Schemas, synthetic example artefacts, the reference validator, automated tests, and the Phase 3 pilot evaluation report. The implementation demonstrates reproducible structural evaluation of asserted delegated authority. It does not establish the legal or institutional validity of that authority, authenticate cryptographic evidence, represent officially approved AUT governance architecture, or demonstrate integration with live university identity and access-management systems. The AUT CISRC implementation-profile schemas differ from the original SILT Core v0.1 JSON Schemas and should not be interpreted as direct normative schema conformance. This research output is separate from the historical SILT Core v0.1 release of April 2026 and the subsequent SILT Core v0.2 Semantic Architecture. Funding acknowledgement: This open research project was supported by Stichting Vietsch (Vietsch Foundation). Project lead: Gareth Farry. Source repository and versioned release: https://github.com/Sugarlicks/silt-identity-core/releases/tag/aut-cisrc-v0.1-pilot-2026

publications.title: Branch‐and‐Cut POPMUSIC for the Electric Vehicle Routing Problem With Time Windows
publications.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Advancements in computer hardware and commercial software have enabled the use of branch‐and‐cut (BC) methodologies to address medium‐scale vehicle routing problems (VRPs). Despite the introduction of efficient heuristics in the literature, tailoring these approaches to suit various VRP variants, such as the electric vehicle routing problem with time windows (EVRPTW), remains a difficult task. EVRPTW is an extension of the classic VRP with time windows in which internal combustion engine vehicles are replaced by electric vehicles. In this study, we develop a POPMUSIC matheuristic to solve the EVRPTW that relies solely on BC (termed BC‐POPMUSIC), and can be implemented using commercial optimisation software such as Gurobi. We introduce new battery infeasibility inequalities, along with capacity cuts, reachability cuts, ‐path cuts and polar cuts, and incorporate them into Gurobi to tighten the linear programming (LP) relaxation of the mixed integer linear program (MILP) model. Through extensive experiments, we show that this tightening can improve the quality of solutions. Since the EVRPTW requires visits to recharging stations when the battery is depleted, we propose an improvement heuristic to efficiently manage these recharging stops. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BC‐POPMUSIC on known benchmark instances of EVRPTW and compare it with state‐of‐the‐art exact solutions. Our result shows that the approach achieves comparable or better performance, especially on larger problems. In addition, we present new best known solutions for several benchmark instances.

publications.title: Near-optimal universal scheduling for moldable tasks: the Fair algorithm
publications.abstract:
Abstract
                  The problem of scheduling moldable tasks on multiprocessor systems with the goal of minimizing the makespan has received significant attention, especially in contexts where tasks have dependence constraints (task graphs) or arrive dynamically (online scheduling). However, the combined setting—online scheduling of moldable task graphs—remains less explored. Prior studies have addressed this problem by designing algorithms specifically tailored to particular speedup models, such as Amdahl, Communication, or Roofline. Although these specialized algorithms achieve constant competitive ratios under their respective models, their applicability is limited in practice: Each requires tasks to adhere to a predefined speedup model. In this paper, we introduce a novel, universal online algorithm capable of handling arbitrary monotonic moldable tasks without assumptions about their speedup behavior. Remarkably, when applied to the specific speedup models previously studied, our algorithm achieves competitive ratios comparable to—or better than—those obtained by the specialized algorithms. For the General and Power Communication models, we further show that the optimal simultaneous time-and-area factor is 2, matching the Amdahl case.

publications.title: From hardware to software: in-vehicle interface complaints in China, 2019-2026 (dataset and code)
publications.abstract: This repository contains the aggregated data, validation labels, analysis code, and figure code for the study "From hardware to software: a seven-year computational analysis of in-vehicle interface complaints in China." The study examines how owner complaints about in-vehicle interfaces changed between 2019 and 2026. We assembled 23,699 owner reviews of 120 vehicle models from 41 brands in the Chinese market and coded each review for the presence and category of interface complaint using a large language model, validated against 150 independently human-coded reviews (Cohen's kappa = 0.757). Contents:- data/model_level_aggregates.csv: model-by-period aggregates (review counts, interface complaint counts by category, median screen size, mean purchase price)- data/validation_150.csv: human and model labels for the validation sample (no review text)- data/sample_120_models.csv: the sampled models and their metadata- code/: retrieval, coding, and analysis scripts, including the full coding prompt- figures/: source data, plotting code, and 300-dpi figures All files are deposited at the top level of this record: the paths data/, code/, and figures/ in README.md correspond to the file names listed above. Raw review text is not redistributed because it is user-generated content owned by its authors. The retrieval scripts allow the corpus to be reconstructed from the public source, subject to the platform's terms of service. Code is released under the MIT License; data and figures under CC BY 4.0.

publications.title: Forensic Reconstruction of Web-Based Social Media Account Takeover via Credential Phishing
publications.abstract: Credential phishing against browser-authenticated accounts can produce fragmented digital traces across browser storage, phishing infrastructure, network traffic, and account activity records. This study aims to reconstruct a Discord Web account takeover caused by credential phishing through multi-source forensic correlation. Evidence was obtained from Chrome browser artifacts, phishing server logs, Wireshark network captures, and documentation of attacker-side account activity within a controlled experimental scenario. The forensic analysis recovered 10 of 12 expected artifacts, resulting in an Artifact Recovery Rate (ARR) of 83.3%, while 4 of 6 incident stages were supported by at least two evidence items or source layers, producing an Evidence Corroboration Score (ECS) of 66.7%. The reconstructed timeline covers six stages of the incident, from the delivery of a phishing link to the confirmation of account access. The study introduces ARR and ECS as quantitative measures for evaluating artifact recovery and cross-source evidence corroboration. The findings further demonstrate that browser artifacts alone are insufficient to establish a complete account takeover sequence, and that correlation among browser, server, network, and account activity evidence is necessary to construct a coherent and verifiable forensic timeline. These results provide a practical basis for incident responders and forensic examiners to correlate heterogeneous evidence sources when investigating browser-mediated credential phishing.
